title: Loop and tooth: ص ض

bigIdea.text: ص (ṣad) and ض (ḍad) share one body: an oval loop with a small tooth. Both are heavy. No dot = ṣad, a heavy 's'. One dot above = ḍad, made with the side of the tongue.

proper.text: Both have an oval loop followed by a small tooth; standing alone or at the end of a word they also have a round tail below the line. ض has one dot above the loop.

Sounds: ص is a heavy 's'. The tongue tip sits where it does for س, but the back of the tongue rises and the tongue presses up toward the roof of the mouth, so the sound is deep and full. ض is heavy and voiced, made with the side of the tongue pressed along the upper back teeth. Never replace it with a light د or with ظ; copy your teacher and Minshawi for it.

Sifat: both are 'raised' (isti'la: the tongue rises toward the roof of the mouth) and 'closed' (itbaq: the tongue and the roof of the mouth meet). ص is whispered (hams) and has a whistle (safir). ض holds the breath back (jahr) and has 'stretching' (istitala): its sound runs along the edge of the tongue.

proper.text: Heavy or light: both are heavy. They are two of the seven heavy letters (خ ص ض غ ط ق ظ).

Common mistakes. Persian/Urdu readers: ص is read as س and ض as 'z' (like ز), so both lose their weight and ض loses its own place. English speakers: ص comes out as a plain 's' and ض as a plain 'd'. Fix: first find the heavy sound by raising the back of the tongue, then keep it for the whole letter.

points.detail: Tip of the tongue with the front teeth (shared with س and ز)
Side of the tongue pressed against the upper molars

memoryHook.text: Loop and tooth means heavy; a dot turns ṣad into ḍad.

extras.text: Linguists think the old ض was made along the side of the tongue; in most modern spoken Arabic it has become a heavy 'd'-like stop.
Arabic is often called 'the language of ḍad', because this letter is so distinctive.

tip.text: ص: tongue tip at the front teeth, whispered, with a whistle. ض: the side of the tongue along the upper back teeth, voiced, no whistle. Keep both heavy.

questions.q: Which letter is an oval loop and tooth with one dot above?
explain: Right: the loop and tooth with a dot is ḍad.
ṣad is the same body with no dot.
ẓa also has a loop and a dot, but a tall upright stroke instead of the tooth.
fa has a small round head with one dot, not an oval loop with a tooth.

questions.q: Are ص and ض heavy or light?
explain: Right: both are among the seven heavy letters.
Neither is light.
ḍad is heavy too.

options: The side of the tongue pressed against the upper molars
Tongue against the roots of the upper front teeth
Tongue against the edges of the upper front teeth
explain: Right: ḍad has its own place along the side of the tongue.
That is the place of د, ت and ط.
That is the place of ذ, ث and ظ.
That is the place of ع and ح.

questions.q: Which quality belongs to ض alone?
options: Stretching (istitala): the sound runs along the edge of the tongue
explain: Right: istitala is ḍad's own quality.
The whistle belongs to ص ز س.
Spreading of air belongs to ش.
Repetition belongs to ر.

explain: Right: in Persian and Urdu ḍad is read as 'z'.
A plain 'd' is the usual English-speaker slip, not the Persian/Urdu one.
ṣad is a different heavy letter: whispered and whistling.
ṭa is a different heavy letter, made at the roots of the upper front teeth.

options: Raising the back of the tongue so the sound becomes deep and heavy
Moving the tongue to the edges of the front teeth
explain: Right: same tongue tip, heavier body.
Adding voice to س gives ز, not ص.
That gives ث.
The lips are not used for these letters.

questions.q: How do you tell ص from ض?
options: ض has one dot above; ص has none
You can't; they are the same letter
explain: Right: the dot is the only difference in shape.
The loops are the same.
Both have one small tooth.
They are different letters with different sounds.

options: Tip of the tongue with the front teeth
Side of the tongue against the upper molars
The part of the throat nearest the mouth
explain: Right: ṣad shares this place with س and ز.
That is the place of ض.
That is the place of ج, ش and ي.
That is the place of خ and غ.

explain: Right: ṣad is one of the three whistling letters (ص ز س).
ḍad has stretching (istitala) instead.
Only ṣad whistles.
ṣad does whistle.

The breath goes through the nose
explain: Right: the itbaq letters are ص ض ط ظ.

options: Heavy and voiced, from the side of the tongue along the upper back teeth
A light 'd' from the tongue tip

That is د.
That is ز.

options: Its weight and its own place along the side of the tongue
explain: Right: ḍad is heavy and has its own place.

remnote: ص (ṣad) == Loop + tooth, no dot; tip of the tongue with the front teeth; heavy whispered 's' with a whistle
ض (ḍad) == Loop + tooth, one dot above; side of the tongue against the upper molars; heavy, voiced, stretched
Persian/Urdu fix for ص and ض == ص is a heavy 's' (not س); ض has its own place (not 'z')
